SR = 2πf V_{pk}.title: Slew rate: the full-power bandwidth of an op amp
SR = 2πf V_{pk}.about: An op amp's output can change only so fast, its slew rate SR. A sine of peak V_{pk} and frequency f changes fastest at its zero crossings, at 2πf V_{pk}, so this gives the slew rate a sine needs, or the highest frequency a given op amp can swing to full amplitude without distortion.
assumptions: The output is a sine; a square or triangle wave has a different peak rate of change
SR is the large-signal limit, set by the current that charges the internal compensation capacitor; it is separate from the small-signal gain-bandwidth limit
Above this frequency the output turns into a triangle wave whose amplitude falls with frequency
vars: slew rate, the largest rate of change of the output

example.problem: A 741 op amp slews at 0.5 V/µs. What is the highest frequency at which it can deliver a 10 V peak sine?

CMRR = 20 log_{10}(A_{d}/A_{cm}).title: Common-mode rejection ratio
CMRR = 20 log_{10}(A_{d}/A_{cm}).about: A differential amplifier should amplify the difference between its inputs and ignore what they share. CMRR compares the differential gain with the common-mode gain, in decibels; the higher it is, the better the amplifier rejects noise picked up equally on both inputs.
assumptions: A_{d} and A_{cm} are measured at the same frequency; CMRR falls as frequency rises
In a difference amplifier built from resistors, resistor mismatch usually limits CMRR far below the op amp's own figure
related: output with both kinds of input

example.problem: An amplifier has a differential gain of 200 000 and a common-mode gain of 2. Find its CMRR.

V_{out} = −R_{f} (V_{1}/R_{1} + V_{2}/R_.title: Inverting summing amplifier
V_{out} = −R_{f} (V_{1}/R_{1} + V_{2}/R_.about: Several inputs, each through its own resistor, feed the inverting input of an op amp with feedback resistor R_{f}. The inverting input is a virtual ground, so the input currents add there and flow through R_{f}; the output is a weighted, inverted sum. Used in audio mixers and simple DACs.
assumptions: Ideal op amp: infinite gain and input impedance, so the inverting input sits at 0 V (virtual ground)
Negative feedback is in place and the output stays within the supply rails
The inputs do not interact, because each sees a virtual ground

example.problem: A summing amplifier has R_{f} = 10 kΩ, R_{1} = 10 kΩ and R_{2} = 5 kΩ. The inputs are V_{1} = 1 V and V_{2} = 0.5 V. Find V_{out}.

V_{out} = (R_{2}/R_{1})(V_{2} − V_{1}).title: Difference amplifier
V_{out} = (R_{2}/R_{1})(V_{2} − V_{1}).about: One op amp and four resistors amplify the difference between two voltages. V_{1} goes in through R_{1} to the inverting input, V_{2} through R_{1} to the non-inverting input, which R_{2} ties to ground, and R_{2} is the feedback resistor. Used to measure across a current-sense resistor or bridge.
assumptions: Ideal op amp with negative feedback
The resistors are matched in pairs (R_{2}/R_{1} the same on both sides); any mismatch lets common-mode voltage through and lowers CMRR
The sources driving it see unequal, finite input resistances (R_{1} and R_{1} + R_{2}); use an instrumentation amplifier when that matters
related: how well it ignores what V_{1} and V_{2} share
first stage of a three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier

example.problem: A bridge's outputs are 2.05 V and 2.00 V. A difference amplifier with R_{1} = 10 kΩ and R_{2} = 100 kΩ reads it. Find V_{out}.

V_{out} = −(1/(RC)) ∫ V_{in} dt.title: Op-amp integrator
V_{out} = −(1/(RC)) ∫ V_{in} dt.about: An inverting amplifier with a capacitor in place of the feedback resistor. The input current V_{in}/R charges the capacitor, so the output is the inverted, scaled running integral of the input. A constant input gives a ramp; a square wave gives a triangle wave.
assumptions: Ideal op amp with a virtual ground at the inverting input
Real integrators drift: input offset voltage and bias current are integrated too and slowly saturate the output, so a large resistor is often placed across C to limit the DC gain
The output must stay within the supply rails; the capacitor starts at a known charge (often reset to zero)

example.problem: An integrator has R = 10 kΩ and C = 1 µF, starting with V_{out} = 0. A constant 1 V is applied for 5 ms. Find V_{out}.

V_{out} = −(1/(RC)) ∫ V_{in} dt.try: -1 * (1 V * 5 ms)/(10 kΩ * 1 µF) to V

V_{out} = −RC dV_{in}/dt.title: Op-amp differentiator
V_{out} = −RC dV_{in}/dt.about: An inverting amplifier with a capacitor as the input element and a resistor as feedback. The capacitor's current is C dV_{in}/dt, which flows through R, so the output is the inverted, scaled rate of change of the input. A ramp gives a constant; a triangle wave gives a square wave.
assumptions: Ideal op amp with a virtual ground
Its gain rises with frequency, so it amplifies high-frequency noise and can oscillate; practical circuits add a small resistor in series with C to cap the gain
Steps in the input give spikes limited only by the rails and slew rate

example.problem: A differentiator has R = 10 kΩ and C = 10 nF. Its input ramps up at 1 V per millisecond. Find V_{out}.

V_{out} = −RC dV_{in}/dt.try: -10 kΩ * 10 nF * (1 V / 1 ms) to V

V_{out} = V_{in}.title: Voltage follower (unity-gain buffer)
V_{out} = V_{in}.about: The output is tied straight back to the inverting input, so the op amp makes its output equal its input. The gain is 1, but the input draws almost no current and the output can drive a heavy load, so the buffer stops a load from pulling down a weak source.
assumptions: Ideal op amp: very high input impedance, low output impedance
The output current stays within the op amp's limit and the voltage within its input and output ranges (check rail-to-rail specs)
Unity gain is the hardest case for stability; the op amp must be unity-gain stable
related: what an unbuffered source of resistance R_{s} gives a load R_{L}
non-inverting amplifier; the buffer is R_{f} = 0

example.problem: A 2 V sensor with 100 kΩ internal resistance must drive a 1 kΩ load. Compare the load voltage with and without a buffer.
steps: Without: V_{L} = 2 V × 1 kΩ/(100 kΩ + 1 kΩ) = 19.8 mV
With a buffer the sensor sees a near-infinite load, so V_{out} = V_{in} = 2 V across the 1 kΩ
example.answer: 19.8 mV without the buffer; 2 V with it

V_{out} = V_{in}.try: 2 V * 1 kΩ/(100 kΩ + 1 kΩ) to mV

I = I_{S} (e^{V/(nV_{T})} − 1).title: Shockley diode equation
I = I_{S} (e^{V/(nV_{T})} − 1).about: Gives a pn-junction diode's current for a voltage across it. Forward-biased, the current rises exponentially, about tenfold for every 60 mV (n = 1); reverse-biased, it settles at the tiny saturation current −I_{S}.
assumptions: Valid in forward bias and modest reverse bias, not in reverse breakdown
Ignores series resistance, which flattens the curve at high current
I_{S} roughly doubles every 5 °C, so the forward voltage at fixed current falls about 2 mV/°C
n is 1 for an ideal junction, up to about 2 in real diodes
vars: voltage across the diode, anode to cathode
related: solved for voltage, when I ≫ I_{S}

example.problem: A silicon diode has I_{S} = 10^{−14} A and n = 1 at 300 K (V_{T} = 25.85 mV). Find the current at V = 0.65 V.

V_{T} = kT/q.title: Thermal voltage
V_{T} = kT/q.about: The voltage scale of semiconductor physics: the energy kT of thermal agitation per unit charge. Carriers must climb barriers of this order, so currents change by e for every V_{T} of bias. It appears in the diode equation, BJT transconductance and small-signal resistances. About 25.9 mV at 300 K, often rounded to 25 or 26 mV.
assumptions: T is the junction temperature in kelvin, not the ambient in °C

example.problem: Find the thermal voltage at 300 K.

V_{T} = kT/q.try: boltzmann constant * 300 K / elementary charge to mV

r_{d} = nV_{T}/I_{D}.title: Diode small-signal resistance
r_{d} = nV_{T}/I_{D}.about: For a small signal riding on a DC bias current I_{D}, a diode behaves like a resistor whose value is the slope of its V–I curve at that point. More bias current gives a smaller resistance.
assumptions: The signal is small, a few mV, much less than nV_{T}, so the curve is close to linear
Ignores the diode's series resistance (add it for large currents) and its capacitance (matters at high frequency)
related: the same idea in a BJT

example.problem: A diode with n = 1 is biased at 1 mA at 300 K. Find its small-signal resistance.

V_{dc} = V_{m}/π.title: Half-wave rectifier average output
V_{dc} = V_{m}/π.about: One diode passes only the positive half of each sine cycle. The output's average (DC) value is the sine's peak over π, about 0.318 V_{m}.
assumptions: Resistive load and no filter capacitor
Ideal diode; subtract its forward drop (about 0.7 V) from V_{m} for a real one
V_{m} is the peak, √2 times the RMS rating of a transformer
related: peak inverse voltage on the diode

example.problem: A 12 V (RMS) transformer feeds a half-wave rectifier with an ideal diode and a resistive load. Find the DC output.

V_{dc} = 2V_{m}/π.title: Full-wave rectifier average output
V_{dc} = 2V_{m}/π.about: A bridge or center-tapped rectifier flips the negative half-cycles so both halves reach the load. The average is twice the half-wave value, about 0.637 V_{m}, and the ripple is at twice the line frequency.
assumptions: Resistive load and no filter capacitor
Ideal diodes; a bridge has two diode drops (about 1.4 V) in the path, a center-tapped circuit one
V_{m} is the peak of the (half-)winding voltage
related: ripple once a capacitor is added

example.problem: A 12 V (RMS) transformer feeds a bridge rectifier with ideal diodes and a resistive load. Find the DC output.

V_{r} ≈ I/(fC).title: Capacitor-filter ripple voltage
V_{r} ≈ I/(fC).about: A capacitor after a rectifier holds the output up between peaks, sagging as the load drains it. Between recharges it loses about I/(fC) volts, where f is the rate of the recharging peaks: the line frequency for half-wave, twice it for full-wave.
assumptions: The ripple is small next to V_{m}, so the load current stays nearly constant and the capacitor discharges for nearly a whole period
Overestimates slightly, since the capacitor actually recharges before the period ends
Large capacitors draw short, high current spikes from the diodes and transformer
vars: ripple frequency (line frequency, or twice it for full-wave)
related: capacitor needed for a ripple target

example.problem: A full-wave rectifier on 60 Hz mains supplies 0.5 A through a 4700 µF filter capacitor. Find the ripple.

I_{C} = β I_{B}.title: BJT current gain in the active region
I_{C} = β I_{B}.about: In the forward-active region a small base current controls a collector current β times larger. This is what makes the BJT an amplifier and a switch.
assumptions: Forward-active region: base-emitter junction forward-biased, base-collector reverse-biased (V_{CE} above about 0.2 V)
β varies widely between parts of the same type (often 50 to 300) and with temperature and current, so good designs don't depend on its exact value
In saturation I_{C} < βI_{B}

example.problem: A transistor with β = 100 has a base current of 20 µA. Find the collector current.

I_{E} = I_{B} + I_{C}.title: BJT terminal currents (Kirchhoff's current law)
I_{E} = I_{B} + I_{C}.about: Everything that enters the base and collector leaves by the emitter (for NPN). Since I_{B} is small, I_{E} is only slightly larger than I_{C}.
assumptions: Holds in every region of operation; it is just Kirchhoff's current law on the transistor
Currents are taken in their normal directions: into base and collector, out of emitter for NPN, the reverse for PNP

example.problem: A BJT in the active region has I_{B} = 20 µA and I_{C} = 2 mA. Find the emitter current.

α = β/(β + 1).title: Common-base current gain α
α = β/(β + 1).about: α is the fraction of the emitter current that reaches the collector, I_{C}/I_{E}. Since I_{E} = I_{C} + I_{B} = I_{C}(1 + 1/β), it follows α = β/(β + 1). It sits just below 1, and a small change in α means a large change in β, which is why β varies so much between parts.
assumptions: Active region, as for β
In most designs take I_{C} ≈ I_{E}; the 1% difference rarely matters

example.problem: A transistor has β = 100. Find α.

I_{C} = I_{S} e^{V_{BE}/V_{T}}.title: BJT collector current vs base-emitter voltage
I_{C} = I_{S} e^{V_{BE}/V_{T}}.about: The collector current depends exponentially on the base-emitter voltage, like a diode. Every 60 mV more V_{BE} gives about ten times the current, which is why V_{BE} stays near 0.6 to 0.7 V over a wide range of currents.
assumptions: Forward-active region, with I_{C} ≫ I_{S} so the −1 of the diode equation is dropped
Ignores the Early effect (I_{C} rising with V_{CE}) and high-injection effects
Strongly temperature-dependent: at fixed I_{C}, V_{BE} falls about 2 mV/°C

example.problem: A BJT has I_{S} = 10^{−15} A. Find I_{C} at V_{BE} = 0.7 V and 300 K (V_{T} = 25.85 mV).

g_{m} = I_{C}/V_{T}.title: BJT transconductance
g_{m} = I_{C}/V_{T}.about: How much the collector current changes per volt of base-emitter signal: the slope of the exponential I_{C}–V_{BE} curve at the bias point. It depends only on the bias current, not on the transistor, and sets the gain of every BJT amplifier.
assumptions: Small-signal: the signal on V_{BE} is much less than V_{T}
Forward-active region

example.problem: A BJT is biased at I_{C} = 1 mA at 300 K. Find g_{m}.

r_{π} = β/g_{m}.title: BJT small-signal input resistance r_{π}
r_{π} = β/g_{m}.about: The resistance looking into the base, with the emitter grounded, in the hybrid-π model. A base-voltage signal v_{be} drives a base current v_{be}/r_{π}, which is β times smaller than the collector's g_{m} v_{be}.
assumptions: Small-signal, forward-active region
Low frequency, so the junction capacitances are ignored

example.problem: A BJT with β = 100 is biased at I_{C} = 1 mA (g_{m} = 38.7 mS). Find r_{π}.

r_{o} = V_{A}/I_{C}.title: Output resistance from the Early effect
r_{o} = V_{A}/I_{C}.about: The collector current creeps up as V_{CE} grows (the Early effect), so the transistor's output is not a perfect current source but one with a resistance r_{o} in parallel. Extend the I_{C}–V_{CE} curves backward and they meet at −V_{A}.
assumptions: Small-signal, forward-active region
V_{A} (Early voltage) is typically 50 to 150 V for discrete parts, less in small IC devices
related: the Early effect in the large-signal equation

example.problem: A BJT with V_{A} = 100 V is biased at I_{C} = 1 mA. Find r_{o}.

A_{v} = −g_{m} (R_{C} ∥ r_{o}).title: Common-emitter amplifier gain
A_{v} = −g_{m} (R_{C} ∥ r_{o}).about: In a common-emitter stage, the input drives the base, the emitter is grounded for signals, and the output is taken at the collector. The signal current g_{m} v_{be} flows through R_{C} in parallel with r_{o}, giving a large, inverted voltage gain.
assumptions: Small-signal, forward-active region
Emitter fully bypassed to ground for signals; an unbypassed R_{E} lowers the gain to about −R_{C}/R_{E}
No load resistor; a load R_{L} goes in parallel with R_{C} and r_{o}
Midband frequencies: coupling capacitors short, device capacitances open

example.problem: A common-emitter stage is biased at I_{C} = 1 mA (g_{m} = 38.7 mS) with R_{C} = 5 kΩ and r_{o} = 100 kΩ. Find A_{v}.

V_{ov} = V_{GS} − V_{th}.title: MOSFET overdrive voltage
V_{ov} = V_{GS} − V_{th}.about: How far the gate-source voltage is above threshold. It sets how strongly the channel conducts: the MOSFET is off when V_{ov} ≤ 0, and the drain current and transconductance grow with it.
assumptions: NMOS (for PMOS use the magnitudes, |V_{GS}| − |V_{th}|)
V_{th} rises with source-body voltage (body effect) and falls with temperature
Check saturation with V_{DS} ≥ V_{ov}, not V_{DS} ≥ V_{GS}

example.problem: An NMOS transistor has V_{th} = 0.6 V and V_{GS} = 1.0 V. Find its overdrive.

I_{D} = (1/2) μ_{n} C_{ox} (W/L) V_{ov}^.title: MOSFET drain current in saturation (square law)
I_{D} = (1/2) μ_{n} C_{ox} (W/L) V_{ov}^.about: Once the channel is pinched off at the drain, the drain current stops depending on V_{DS} and grows with the square of the overdrive. This is the region used for amplifiers and current sources.
assumptions: Saturation: V_{ov} > 0 and V_{DS} ≥ V_{ov}
Long-channel square law; short-channel devices follow it loosely (velocity saturation makes I_{D} closer to linear in V_{ov})
Ignores channel-length modulation; multiply by (1 + λV_{DS}) to include it

example.problem: An NMOS has μ_{n}C_{ox} = 200 µA/V^{2}, W/L = 10 and V_{ov} = 0.4 V, in saturation. Find I_{D}.

V_{DS} ≥ V_{ov}.title: Condition for MOSFET saturation
V_{DS} ≥ V_{ov}.about: A MOSFET is in saturation, acting as a current source, only while the drain voltage is high enough to pinch off the channel at the drain: V_{DS} at least the overdrive. Below that it is in triode and acts like a resistor. Check this after every saturation calculation.
assumptions: NMOS with V_{ov} > 0; for PMOS use |V_{DS}| ≥ |V_{ov}|
Equivalent to V_{GD} ≤ V_{th}: the gate is not more than a threshold above the drain
related: drain voltage with a drain resistor

example.problem: An NMOS with V_{ov} = 0.4 V carries I_{D} = 160 µA from a 1.8 V supply through a drain resistor R_{D}. What is the largest R_{D} that keeps it in saturation?

I_{D} = μ_{n} C_{ox} (W/L) (V_{ov} V_{DS.title: MOSFET drain current in the triode region
I_{D} = μ_{n} C_{ox} (W/L) (V_{ov} V_{DS.about: With a small drain voltage the channel runs the full length and the MOSFET acts as a voltage-controlled resistor. For very small V_{DS} the current is nearly linear in V_{DS}; this is the region a MOSFET switch sits in when on.
assumptions: Triode: V_{ov} > 0 and V_{DS} < V_{ov}
Long-channel model
At V_{DS} = V_{ov} it meets the saturation equation

example.problem: An NMOS with μ_{n}C_{ox} = 200 µA/V^{2}, W/L = 10 and V_{ov} = 0.4 V has V_{DS} = 0.1 V. Find I_{D}.

g_{m} = 2I_{D}/V_{ov}.title: MOSFET transconductance
g_{m} = 2I_{D}/V_{ov}.about: How much the drain current changes per volt of gate signal, at the bias point: the slope of the square-law curve. For a given current, a smaller overdrive gives more g_{m}.
assumptions: Saturation region, small signal
Long-channel square law; short-channel devices give somewhat less

example.problem: An NMOS is biased at I_{D} = 160 µA with V_{ov} = 0.4 V. Find g_{m}.

r_{o} = 1/(λ I_{D}).title: MOSFET output resistance (channel-length modulation)
r_{o} = 1/(λ I_{D}).about: In saturation the drain current still rises slightly with V_{DS}, because the pinched-off part of the channel grows and shortens the effective length. That slope is modeled as a resistance r_{o} from drain to source.
assumptions: Saturation region, small signal
λ is larger for short channels, roughly proportional to 1/L

example.problem: An NMOS with λ = 0.05 V^{−1} is biased at I_{D} = 160 µA. Find r_{o}.

A_{v} = −g_{m} (R_{D} ∥ r_{o}).title: Common-source amplifier gain
A_{v} = −g_{m} (R_{D} ∥ r_{o}).about: The MOSFET counterpart of the common-emitter stage: input at the gate, source grounded for signals, output at the drain. The signal current g_{m} v_{gs} through R_{D} in parallel with r_{o} gives an inverted voltage gain.
assumptions: Saturation region, small signal
Source fully bypassed; an unbypassed R_{S} lowers the gain to about −g_{m}R_{D}/(1 + g_{m}R_{S})
No load; a load R_{L} goes in parallel too
Midband frequencies
related: intrinsic gain, with an ideal current-source load

example.problem: A common-source stage has g_{m} = 0.8 mS, R_{D} = 5 kΩ and r_{o} = 125 kΩ. Find A_{v}.

P = a C V^{2} f.title: CMOS dynamic (switching) power
P = a C V^{2} f.about: Each time a CMOS node switches, its capacitance is charged from the supply and then discharged to ground, spending CV^{2} per full cycle. Multiplied by the clock rate and the fraction of nodes that switch, it gives the chip's switching power. The V^{2} is why lowering the supply saves so much power.
assumptions: Counts only switching power; leakage (static) and short-circuit current are extra
C is the total switched capacitance; a is the activity factor, the fraction switching each cycle (some texts put a 1/2 here and define a per transition)
Rail-to-rail swings at the supply voltage V

example.problem: A processor has 1 nF of switched capacitance, a 1.0 V supply and a 2 GHz clock, and 10 % of its nodes switch each cycle. Find its dynamic power.

¬(A · B) = ¬A + ¬B.title: De Morgan's law: NOT of an AND
¬(A · B) = ¬A + ¬B.about: Inverting an AND is the same as ORing the inverted inputs. In gates: a NAND is an OR with bubbles on its inputs. It lets you move inversions through a circuit and build any logic from NAND gates alone.
assumptions: Holds for any Boolean values; extends to any number of inputs: ¬(A · B · C) = ¬A + ¬B + ¬C

example.problem: Simplify ¬(A · ¬B) and check it at A = 1, B = 0.
steps: At A = 1, B = 0: left side ¬(1 · 1) = 0; right side 0 + 0 = 0

¬(A + B) = ¬A · ¬B.title: De Morgan's law: NOT of an OR
¬(A + B) = ¬A · ¬B.about: Inverting an OR is the same as ANDing the inverted inputs. A NOR gate equals an AND gate with inverted inputs, so NOR alone can also build any logic.
assumptions: Holds for any Boolean values and any number of inputs

example.problem: An alarm is silent when neither door A nor window B is open: S = ¬(A + B). Write it as an AND and check it at A = 0, B = 0.

A ⊕ B = A · ¬B + ¬A · B.title: Exclusive OR (XOR)
A ⊕ B = A · ¬B + ¬A · B.about: XOR is 1 when exactly one input is 1, i.e. when the inputs differ. It is the sum bit of a binary adder, the heart of parity checks, and a controlled inverter: A ⊕ 1 = ¬A, A ⊕ 0 = A.
assumptions: Associative and commutative, so a chain of XORs gives 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1
related: S = A ⊕ B, C = A · B

example.problem: Find the even-parity bit for the byte 1011 0010.
steps: There are four 1s, an even count, so the result is 0
Parity bit 0 keeps the total number of 1s even

0 to 2^{n} − 1.title: Range of an n-bit unsigned integer
0 to 2^{n} − 1.about: n bits give 2^{n} different patterns, since each bit doubles the count. Read as an unsigned number they cover 0 up to 2^{n} − 1: the top is one less than 2^{n} because zero uses a pattern. Adding past the top wraps around to 0 (overflow).
assumptions: Plain binary; each bit k has weight 2^{k}

example.problem: What is the largest value an 8-bit and a 16-bit unsigned integer can hold?

−2^{n−1} to 2^{n−1} − 1.title: Range of an n-bit two's-complement integer
−2^{n−1} to 2^{n−1} − 1.about: Two's complement gives the top bit a weight of −2^{n−1}, so half the patterns are negative. There is one more negative number than positive, and the same adder works for signed and unsigned numbers. To negate, invert every bit and add 1.
assumptions: Overflow happens when two numbers of the same sign add to a result of the other sign
vars: number of bits, including the sign bit

example.problem: What range does an 8-bit two's-complement integer cover?

T_{clk} ≥ t_{cq} + t_{logic} + t_{su}.title: Setup-time constraint on the clock period
T_{clk} ≥ t_{cq} + t_{logic} + t_{su}.about: Data launched from one flip-flop on a clock edge must get through the logic and settle at the next flip-flop before that flip-flop's setup window closes. The slowest such path, the critical path, sets the shortest clock period.
assumptions: Uses the worst-case (maximum) delays
Ignores clock skew and jitter; skew that delays the capturing clock adds to the budget, the other way subtracts
A separate hold-time check uses the shortest path: t_{cq} + t_{logic,min} ≥ t_{hold}
vars: setup time of the capturing flip-flop

example.problem: A path has t_{cq} = 50 ps, 800 ps of logic and t_{su} = 30 ps. Find the shortest clock period.

f_{max} = 1/T_{clk}.title: Maximum clock frequency
f_{max} = 1/T_{clk}.about: The fastest clock a synchronous circuit can run at is the inverse of its shortest safe clock period. That period is set by the critical path: the slowest register-to-register route, which must launch, compute and settle before the next edge.
assumptions: T_{clk} is the minimum period from the setup constraint, including clock skew and jitter margin
Use the worst-case (slow corner) delays, not typical ones
Hold time does not limit f_{max}; it is a separate check that holds at any frequency

example.problem: A path has t_{cq} = 120 ps, 700 ps of logic and t_{su} = 60 ps. Find f_{max}.

LSB = V_{FS}/2^{n}.title: Converter resolution: one LSB
LSB = V_{FS}/2^{n}.about: An n-bit ADC or DAC splits its full-scale range into 2^{n} steps. One least-significant bit is the size of each step, the smallest change it can resolve.
assumptions: Ideal converter; real ones add offset, gain error and nonlinearity
Some texts divide by 2^{n} − 1 so the top code reaches full scale exactly

example.problem: A 12-bit ADC has a 3.3 V full-scale range. Find one LSB.

V_{out} = V_{ref} D/2^{n}.title: DAC output for a digital code
V_{out} = V_{ref} D/2^{n}.about: An ideal n-bit DAC outputs its code D as that fraction of the reference voltage. The top code 2^{n} − 1 gives one LSB short of V_{ref}.
assumptions: Ideal, unipolar DAC
D is the unsigned code, 0 to 2^{n} − 1

example.problem: A 10-bit DAC with a 5 V reference receives code 300. Find V_{out}.

SNR = 6.02n + 1.76 dB.title: Ideal ADC signal-to-noise ratio
SNR = 6.02n + 1.76 dB.about: The best SNR an n-bit converter can reach with a full-scale sine input, when quantization error is the only noise. Each extra bit adds about 6 dB.
assumptions: Full-scale sine input; smaller signals lose SNR in proportion
Quantization error is uniform and uncorrelated with the signal; real converters fall short, described by the effective number of bits
related: effective number of bits from a measured SINAD

example.problem: Find the ideal SNR of a 12-bit ADC.

f_{s} ≥ 2 f_{max}.title: Nyquist sampling criterion
f_{s} ≥ 2 f_{max}.about: To capture a signal without aliasing, sample it at more than twice its highest frequency. Anything above f_{s}/2 (the Nyquist frequency) folds back and is indistinguishable from a lower frequency.
assumptions: Strictly greater than 2f_{max} for a sine exactly at f_{max}
Assumes the input is band-limited; an anti-aliasing filter before the ADC enforces it, and its finite roll-off is why real systems sample faster than 2f_{max}

example.problem: Audio extends to 20 kHz. Find the minimum sampling rate, and say why CDs use 44.1 kHz.
steps: 44.1 kHz leaves room for the anti-aliasing filter to roll off between 20 and 22.05 kHz

f_{a} = |f − k f_{s}|.title: Aliased frequency
f_{a} = |f − k f_{s}|.about: A tone above the Nyquist frequency appears after sampling at a lower frequency: its distance to the nearest multiple of the sampling rate. Choose the integer k that brings f_{a} between 0 and f_{s}/2.
assumptions: Ideal sampling, no anti-aliasing filter
A real sine; the sign of the frequency is lost

example.problem: A 7 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz. At what frequency does it appear?
steps: Nyquist frequency is 5 kHz, so 7 kHz aliases

dB = 10 log_{10}(P_{2}/P_{1}).title: Decibels from a power ratio
dB = 10 log_{10}(P_{2}/P_{1}).about: A ratio of two powers in decibels. Gains add and losses subtract on this scale, which is why it is used through whole signal chains. +3 dB doubles the power, +10 dB is ten times.
assumptions: Both are powers, in the same units
A negative result is a loss

example.problem: An amplifier turns a 50 mW input into 2 W. Find its gain in dB.

dB = 20 log_{10}(V_{2}/V_{1}).title: Decibels from a voltage ratio
dB = 20 log_{10}(V_{2}/V_{1}).about: Power goes as voltage squared, so a voltage ratio in dB uses 20 log rather than 10 log. ×2 in voltage is +6 dB, ×10 is +20 dB. Used for amplifier gain and Bode plots.
assumptions: Strictly gives the power ratio only when both voltages are across the same resistance; it is used for voltage gain regardless
Use RMS (or both peak) values, consistently

example.problem: An amplifier turns a 50 mV input into 2 V. Find its voltage gain in dB.

dBm = 10 log_{10}(P/(1 mW)).title: Power in dBm
dBm = 10 log_{10}(P/(1 mW)).about: An absolute power level in decibels relative to 1 mW. 0 dBm is 1 mW, 30 dBm is 1 W. Used in RF and telecom, where gains in dB simply add to it.
assumptions: P in the same units as the 1 mW reference
dBW uses 1 W instead: dBm = dBW + 30

example.problem: Express 50 mW in dBm.

v_{n} = √(4 k T R B).title: Thermal (Johnson–Nyquist) noise of a resistor
v_{n} = √(4 k T R B).about: Every resistor above absolute zero produces a random noise voltage from the thermal motion of its electrons. Its RMS value grows with the square root of resistance, temperature and bandwidth, and sets the noise floor of sensitive amplifiers.
assumptions: White noise, the same per hertz at all practical frequencies
B is the noise bandwidth, slightly wider than the −3 dB bandwidth of a real filter
Excess (1/f) noise in some resistor types comes on top
related: noise density, V/√Hz (about 4 nV/√Hz for 1 kΩ)

example.problem: Find the RMS noise of a 1 kΩ resistor at 300 K over a 20 kHz audio bandwidth.

v_{n} = √(4 k T R B).try: sqrt(4 * boltzmann constant * 300 K * 1 kΩ * 20 kHz) to µV

P_{n} = kTB.title: Available thermal noise power
P_{n} = kTB.about: The noise power a resistor delivers into a matched load, independent of its resistance. At 290 K it is −174 dBm per hertz, the floor every receiver's sensitivity is measured against.
assumptions: Matched load
White noise over bandwidth B
T is the source's noise temperature; 290 K is the standard reference
related: the same in dBm at 290 K

example.problem: Find the thermal noise power at 290 K in a 1 MHz bandwidth, in watts and dBm.

P_{n} = kTB.try: boltzmann constant * 290 K * 1 MHz to W

F = SNR_{in}/SNR_{out}.title: Noise factor
F = SNR_{in}/SNR_{out}.about: Every amplifier adds some noise, so the signal-to-noise ratio gets worse through it. The noise factor is how many times worse; in dB it is the noise figure, NF = 10 log_{10} F. A perfect amplifier has F = 1 (0 dB).
assumptions: SNR values are linear power ratios, not dB
Defined with the input noise at the standard 290 K

example.problem: A receiver stage has an input SNR of 10 000 and an output SNR of 5000. Find F and the noise figure.

C = B log_{2}(1 + S/N).title: Shannon channel capacity
C = B log_{2}(1 + S/N).about: The highest data rate any coding scheme can push through a channel of bandwidth B with signal-to-noise ratio S/N with arbitrarily few errors. Real systems approach but never exceed it.
assumptions: Additive white Gaussian noise
S/N is a linear power ratio, not dB
A theoretical limit; it says nothing about how to build the code

example.problem: A 1 MHz channel has an SNR of 20 dB. Find its capacity.

P_{r} = P_{t} G_{t} G_{r} (λ/(4πd))^{2}.title: Friis transmission equation
P_{r} = P_{t} G_{t} G_{r} (λ/(4πd))^{2}.about: The power a receiving antenna collects from a transmitter a distance d away in free space. The (λ/(4πd))^{2} term, the free-space path loss, falls off with the square of distance and of frequency.
assumptions: Free space, line of sight, no reflections or obstructions
Far field: d much larger than the antennas and than λ
Antennas matched in impedance and polarization; gains as linear ratios, not dBi

example.problem: A 2.4 GHz link transmits 100 mW through two 3 dBi antennas (gain 2 each) over 100 m. Find the received power.

P_{r} = P_{t} G_{t} G_{r} (λ/(4πd))^{2}.try: 0.1 W * 2 * 2 * (speed of light / 2.4 GHz / (4 pi * 100 m))^2 to nW

c = f λ.title: Wave speed, frequency and wavelength
c = f λ.about: An electromagnetic wave travels one wavelength each cycle, so its speed is frequency times wavelength. In vacuum the speed is c; in a cable or dielectric it is slower, v = c/√ε_{r}, and the wavelength shrinks with it.
assumptions: Vacuum (or air, to within 0.03 %)
In a cable or on a PCB the wavelength is shorter by √ε_{r}; using c there oversizes antennas and stubs

example.problem: Find the free-space wavelength of a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi signal.

c = f λ.try: speed of light / 2.4 GHz to cm

Z_{0} = √(L′/C′).title: Characteristic impedance of a lossless line
Z_{0} = √(L′/C′).about: A transmission line's distributed inductance and capacitance per length give it a characteristic impedance: the ratio of voltage to current in a wave travelling one way along it. A load equal to Z_{0} absorbs the wave with no reflection.
assumptions: Lossless line (R′ and G′ negligible); the general form is √((R′ + jωL′)/(G′ + jωC′))
Uniform line, TEM mode
Independent of length and, for a lossless line, of frequency
related: coaxial cable, diameters D and d

example.problem: A coaxial cable has L′ = 250 nH/m and C′ = 100 pF/m. Find Z_{0}.

v_{p} = 1/√(L′C′).title: Phase velocity on a lossless line
v_{p} = 1/√(L′C′).about: How fast a signal travels along a transmission line, set by its inductance and capacitance per length. In a cable it is c/√ε_{r} of the insulation, typically 0.66c for solid polyethylene.
assumptions: Lossless line, TEM mode
Non-magnetic dielectric, so L′C′ = ε_{r}/c^{2}

example.problem: A cable has L′ = 250 nH/m and C′ = 100 pF/m. Find its phase velocity.

β = 2π/λ.title: Phase constant (wavenumber)
β = 2π/λ.about: How many radians of phase a wave goes through per metre of travel. It turns a line's length into an electrical length βl, the angle that appears in the input-impedance formula.
assumptions: λ is the wavelength on the line or in the medium, not in free space unless the wave is in free space
Lossless line; in a lossy line β is the imaginary part of γ = α + jβ

example.problem: A line with v_{p} = 2 × 10^{8} m/s carries 100 MHz. Find β.

Γ = (Z_{L} − Z_{0})/(Z_{L} + Z_{0}).title: Reflection coefficient at a load
Γ = (Z_{L} − Z_{0})/(Z_{L} + Z_{0}).about: When a wave on a line reaches a load that doesn't match Z_{0}, part of it reflects. Γ is the ratio of reflected to incident voltage: 0 for a matched load, −1 for a short, +1 for an open.
assumptions: Z_{L} and Z_{0} may be complex, and so may Γ
|Γ| ≤ 1 for a passive load

example.problem: A 75 Ω antenna is fed by 50 Ω cable. Find Γ and the fraction of power reflected.

VSWR = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|).title: Voltage standing-wave ratio
VSWR = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|).about: Incident and reflected waves add in phase at some points and cancel at others, a standing wave along the line. Its maximum is 1 + |Γ| and its minimum 1 − |Γ| times the incident amplitude, so VSWR is their ratio: 1 for a perfect match, growing without limit toward a short or open. It is easy to measure, so antennas are often specified by it (VSWR < 2 means under 11% of power reflected).
assumptions: Lossless line between the load and where it is measured; loss makes VSWR look better than it is at the load
related: return loss, the same in dB

example.problem: A 50 Ω antenna measures 75 Ω (resistive) at its feed. Find |Γ|, the VSWR and the fraction of power reflected.

Z_{in} = Z_{0} (Z_{L} + jZ_{0} tan(βl))/.title: Input impedance of a lossless line
Z_{in} = Z_{0} (Z_{L} + jZ_{0} tan(βl))/.about: A length of line between a source and a load transforms the load impedance into something else, depending on the line's electrical length βl. This is the basis of stub matching and quarter-wave transformers.
assumptions: Lossless line
βl in radians; the pattern repeats every half wavelength
Special cases: a matched load gives Z_{0} at any length; a quarter wave gives Z_{0}^{2}/Z_{L}; a half wave gives Z_{L}

example.problem: A 100 Ω load sits at the end of an eighth-wavelength of 50 Ω line. Find the input impedance.
steps: l = λ/8, so βl = π/4 and tan(βl) = 1

C = εA/d.title: Parallel-plate capacitance
C = εA/d.about: Two flat plates of area A separated by a gap d store charge in proportion to voltage. A voltage V sets up a field V/d in the gap, and the charge needed to make it is εA·V/d. Capacitance grows with plate area and with the permittivity of the material between them, and falls as the gap widens.
assumptions: Gap small compared to the plate size, so fringing at the edges is negligible
Uniform, linear dielectric filling the gap
ε = ε_{r}ε_{0}: forgetting ε_{0} gives an answer 10^{11} too big; convert cm^{2} and mm to m

example.problem: Two 1 cm^{2} plates are 0.1 mm apart in air. Find the capacitance.

C = εA/d.try: vacuum permittivity * 1 cm^2 / 0.1 mm to pF

L = μN^{2}A/l.title: Inductance of a long solenoid
L = μN^{2}A/l.about: A coil of N turns wound along a length l. Each turn adds to the field and each turn links it, so the inductance grows with N^{2}. A magnetic core multiplies it by the core's relative permeability.
assumptions: Long solenoid: length much greater than diameter, so the field inside is uniform and the ends don't matter (short coils have less)
Linear core material, not saturated

example.problem: An air-core solenoid has 100 turns, a cross-section of 1 cm^{2} and a length of 5 cm. Find its inductance.

L = μN^{2}A/l.try: vacuum permeability * 100^2 * 1 cm^2 / 5 cm to µH

δ = √(2/(ωμσ)).title: Skin depth
δ = √(2/(ωμσ)).about: AC current crowds toward a conductor's surface. The skin depth is how far in the current density falls to 1/e (37 %) of its surface value. At high frequency only a thin skin carries current, raising the resistance.
assumptions: Good conductor (σ ≫ ωε)
Conductor thicker than a few skin depths; flat or large-radius surface
related: the same in terms of f
AC resistance of a round wire of diameter D ≫ δ

example.problem: Find the skin depth in copper (σ = 5.8 × 10^{7} S/m, μ = μ_{0}) at 1 MHz.

δ = √(2/(ωμσ)).try: sqrt(2/(2 pi * 1 MHz * vacuum permeability * 5.8e7 / (Ω m))) to µm

V = E + I_{a} R_{a}.title: DC motor armature voltage equation
V = E + I_{a} R_{a}.about: The supply voltage across a DC motor's armature splits into the back EMF the spinning rotor generates and the drop across the winding's resistance. At stall E = 0, so the current is limited only by R_{a} and is large.
assumptions: Steady state, so the armature inductance's L dI/dt is zero
Ignores brush drop
As a generator the current reverses: V = E − I_{a}R_{a}

example.problem: A 24 V DC motor with R_{a} = 1.5 Ω draws 2 A. Find the back EMF.

E = k ω.title: Back EMF of a DC motor
E = k ω.about: A spinning armature cuts the field and generates a voltage proportional to speed, opposing the supply. This is what limits a motor's speed and current. With SI units, the same constant k is the torque per amp.
assumptions: Constant field (permanent magnet or fixed field current)
k in V·s/rad equals k in N·m/A
ω in rad/s; datasheets often give k in V per 1000 rpm, which must be converted

example.problem: A motor has k = 0.05 V·s/rad. Find its back EMF at 3000 rpm.

τ = k I_{a}.title: DC motor torque
τ = k I_{a}.about: A DC motor's torque is proportional to its armature current: each conductor in the field feels a force BIL. The constant is the same k as in the back EMF when SI units are used, since power in equals mechanical power out: EI_{a} = τω.
assumptions: Constant field
Ignores friction and armature reaction; the useful shaft torque is less by the friction torque

example.problem: A motor with k = 0.05 N·m/A draws 4 A. Find its torque.

τ = k I_{a}.try: 0.05 N m/A * 4 A to N m

P = τ ω.title: Mechanical power of a rotating shaft
P = τ ω.about: Power delivered by a shaft is its torque times its angular speed, with ω in radians per second. Speed in rpm must be converted first.
assumptions: ω in rad/s (multiply rpm by 2π/60)
Instantaneous; with varying torque use averages carefully

example.problem: A motor delivers 0.2 N·m at 3000 rpm. Find its output power.

n_{s} = 120f/p.title: Synchronous speed of an AC machine
n_{s} = 120f/p.about: The magnetic field in an AC motor's stator rotates at a speed set by the supply frequency and the number of poles. A synchronous motor turns exactly at it; an induction motor runs a little slower.
assumptions: p is the number of poles (not pole pairs)
n_{s} in rpm, f in Hz

example.problem: Find the synchronous speed of a 4-pole motor on 60 Hz.

s = (n_{s} − n)/n_{s}.title: Slip of an induction motor
s = (n_{s} − n)/n_{s}.about: An induction motor's rotor must turn slower than the rotating field for current to be induced in it. Slip is that shortfall as a fraction of synchronous speed: 0 at no load, typically 2–5 % at full load, 1 at standstill.
assumptions: Speeds in the same units
The rotor current's frequency is s f

example.problem: A 4-pole, 60 Hz induction motor runs at 1750 rpm. Find its slip.

η = P_{out}/P_{in}.title: Efficiency
η = P_{out}/P_{in}.about: The fraction of input power that comes out as useful output. The rest is lost as heat in resistance, friction, core and switching losses.
assumptions: Both powers in the same units, measured at the same operating point
0 ≤ η ≤ 1 for a passive device
For AC input use real power, P = V I cos θ, not the apparent V I

example.problem: A motor draws 4 A from 24 V and delivers 80 W of shaft power. Find its efficiency.

V_{out} = D V_{in}.title: Buck converter (step-down)
V_{out} = D V_{in}.about: A switch chops the input at duty cycle D, and an inductor and capacitor average it, so the output is the input scaled by D. Far more efficient than a linear regulator because the switch is either fully on or fully off.
assumptions: Ideal switch, diode and inductor; steady state
Continuous conduction mode: the inductor current never falls to zero (at light loads it does and the output rises above DV_{in})
D is the fraction of each period the switch is on, 0 to 1

example.problem: A buck converter steps 12 V down with a duty cycle of 0.275. Find the output.

V_{out} = V_{in}/(1 − D).title: Boost converter (step-up)
V_{out} = V_{in}/(1 − D).about: The inductor charges from the input while the switch is on and, when it opens, adds its voltage to the input to push current to the output. In steady state the inductor's volt-seconds balance: V_{in}D = (V_{out} − V_{in})(1 − D), which gives V_{in}/(1 − D). The output is always at least the input.
assumptions: Ideal components, steady state, continuous conduction
Real boosts top out around 4–5× because the switch and inductor resistance make the gain fall as D → 1

example.problem: A boost converter runs from 5 V at D = 0.6. Find the output.

V_{out} = −D V_{in}/(1 − D).title: Buck-boost converter (inverting)
V_{out} = −D V_{in}/(1 − D).about: Stores energy in the inductor while the switch is on and dumps it into the output while it is off, giving an output of opposite polarity that can be smaller (D < 0.5) or larger (D > 0.5) than the input.
assumptions: Ideal components, steady state, continuous conduction
The output is negative with respect to the input's common terminal

example.problem: A buck-boost converter runs from 12 V at D = 0.6. Find the output.

T = G/(1 + GH).title: Closed-loop transfer function
T = G/(1 + GH).about: A forward path G with negative feedback H gives an overall transfer function T. When the loop gain GH is large, T ≈ 1/H: the result depends on the feedback, not on the less precise forward gain.
assumptions: Negative feedback (a positive feedback loop has 1 − GH)
Linear, time-invariant blocks

example.problem: An amplifier with forward gain G = 100 has feedback H = 0.1. Find the closed-loop gain.

1 + GH = 0.title: Characteristic equation of a feedback loop
1 + GH = 0.about: The closed-loop poles are the roots of 1 + G(s)H(s) = 0. They decide stability and the transient response: all roots in the left half-plane means stable; complex roots mean an oscillating, decaying response.
assumptions: Linear, time-invariant system with negative feedback (positive feedback gives 1 − GH = 0)
Clear the fractions first to get a polynomial in s
It is the open-loop GH that goes in, but the roots are closed-loop poles; don't confuse them with the poles of G

example.problem: A unity-feedback loop has G(s) = 5/(s(s + 2)). Find the closed-loop poles.
steps: Both in the left half-plane: stable, oscillating at 2 rad/s while decaying

e_{ss} = 1/(1 + K_{p}).title: Steady-state error to a step, type 0
e_{ss} = 1/(1 + K_{p}).about: A type 0 loop (no integrator in G) following a unit step settles short of it by this much. Raising the gain shrinks the error but never removes it; an integrator does.
assumptions: Unity feedback, unit step input
Type 0 open loop (no pole at s = 0)
The closed loop must be stable or there is no steady state
vars: steady-state error, as a fraction of the step

example.problem: A type 0 unity-feedback loop has K_{p} = 9. Find the steady-state error to a unit step.

K_{p} = lim_{s→0} G(s).title: Position (static) error constant
K_{p} = lim_{s→0} G(s).about: The open-loop DC gain: G(s) with s set to zero. It sets the steady-state error to a step. It is infinite when G has an integrator (type 1 or higher), giving zero step error.
assumptions: Unity feedback (with other H, form the equivalent unity-feedback G first)
The closed loop must be stable, or the error never settles
The step error is 1/(1 + K_{p}), not 1/K_{p}

example.problem: Find K_{p} and the step error for G(s) = 20/((s + 1)(s + 4)).

u = K_{p} e + K_{i} ∫ e dt + K_{d} de/dt.title: PID controller in the time domain
u = K_{p} e + K_{i} ∫ e dt + K_{d} de/dt.about: The controller output adds three actions on the error e: proportional (reacts to the present error), integral (removes steady error by accumulating past error) and derivative (damps by reacting to the error's trend).
assumptions: Continuous-time ideal form; digital controllers approximate the integral and derivative
Real controllers filter the derivative (it amplifies noise) and limit the integral when the output saturates (anti-windup)
related: the same in the Laplace domain

example.problem: A PID controller has K_{p} = 2, K_{i} = 0.5 s^{−1}, K_{d} = 0.1 s. Right now e = 3, ∫e dt = 4 s, and de/dt = −1 s^{−1}. Find u.

C(s) = K_{p} + K_{i}/s + K_{d} s.title: PID controller transfer function
C(s) = K_{p} + K_{i}/s + K_{d} s.about: The PID controller in the Laplace domain. The integral term is a pole at the origin, which makes the loop one type higher; the derivative term adds a zero that brings phase lead. Put s = jω to get its frequency response.
assumptions: Ideal form; a real derivative has a filter pole, K_{d}s/(τs + 1)
Some texts use the standard form K_{p}(1 + 1/(T_{i}s) + T_{d}s), where K_{i} = K_{p}/T_{i} and K_{d} = K_{p}T_{d}; check which a tuning rule assumes
related: u = K_{p} e + K_{i} ∫ e dt + K_{d} de/dt

example.problem: With K_{p} = 2, K_{i} = 0.5 and K_{d} = 0.1, find C(jω) at ω = 2 rad/s.
